cues.text: On August 15, 1996, the Feast of the Assumption, at the Parish of Santa Maria in Buenos Aires, Argentina, a parishioner receiving Communion dropped the consecrated Host, then declined to pick it up himself because it appeared soiled.

Another, more attentive worshipper noticed and retrieved it, alerting the parish priest, Father Alejandro Pezet, who followed standard Church procedure by placing the Host in a container of water in the tabernacle, intended to let it dissolve naturally over time.
When the tabernacle was reopened on August 26, the Host had not dissolved as expected; instead it bore reddish stains that continued to grow larger with each passing day.

Father Pezet reported the matter to the auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires, Jorge Bergoglio, who had the Host professionally photographed and then, for reasons that remain unclear, chose not to publicize the event, leaving the Host preserved in its container.
The Host remained in the water for three full years without decomposing — a span far beyond what ordinary bread, even sealed in liquid, would be expected to survive intact.

In 1999, now-Archbishop Bergoglio authorized a formal scientific investigation, overseen by Dr. Ricardo Castanon Gomez, a clinical psychologist specializing in brain chemistry who had previously been a skeptic and later became an active proponent of Eucharistic devotion.
An Unidentified Sample Sent to New York

In October 1999, Castanon Gomez took a sample of the tissue and sent it, without revealing its origin, to Dr. Frederick Zugibe, a cardiologist and forensic pathologist in New York, along with a team of additional specialists.
The analysis identified the sample as a fragment of heart muscle from the wall of the left ventricle.
It showed degenerative changes consistent with a living, distressed heart, and contained white blood cells that had penetrated the tissue.
The examining scientists found this state of preservation inconsistent with three years spent in ordinary, unpreserved water.
Jorge Bergoglio, the archbishop who first received Father Pezet's report and later authorized the scientific study, was elected pope in 2013.
He took the name Francis, giving the Buenos Aires account an unusual afterhistory as one of the few Eucharistic traditions personally overseen at every stage by a future pope.

The Host remains preserved and venerated in Buenos Aires, its documented span of study — from a parishioner's dropped Host to a forensic pathologist's laboratory in New York — among the most extensively examined of any twentieth-century Eucharistic account.
